name: Dihydroxyacetone

lead: Dihydroxyacetone (DHA) is a simple three-carbon sugar and the active ingredient in virtually all sunless tanning lotions, sprays and mousses. It is produced commercially by fermentation or chemical conversion of glycerol.

In looksmaxxing communities it is a common way to add a tan without UV exposure. It gives a temporary golden-brown colour that fades over several days as the outer skin sheds. It provides little or no sun protection, so it does not replace sunscreen.

paras: DHA reacts with free amino groups of proteins and amino acids in the stratum corneum through the Maillard reaction, forming brown pigments called melanoidins. The colour is therefore a surface stain rather than a change in melanin production, and it fades as the keratinised cells exfoliate.

Topical use is considered low risk and DHA is a permitted colour additive for external application in the US. Reviews note it should not be ingested or inhaled, so spray-booth use needs eye, mouth and nose protection, and that long-term and inhalation safety data are limited. Skin irritation or contact allergy is uncommon. Reviews also note that users may overestimate their sun protection, since the colour does not shield against UV.

lead: Dihydroxyacetone (DHA, also called glycerone) is a three-carbon sugar and the active ingredient in most sunless tanning lotions, sprays, mousses, wipes and salon spray tans [1][2]. It darkens the outermost layer of the skin through a Maillard reaction with amino acids in keratin, producing brown pigments called melanoidins; the colour is a surface stain rather than new melanin [1].

The US FDA permits DHA as a colour additive for external application but not for the eyes, lips or mucous membranes, and recommends that users avoid ingesting or inhaling it; sunless tanners are regulated as cosmetics and cannot claim protection from ultraviolet radiation [2]. Reviews note that more safety studies are warranted given how widespread its use is [2][3].

In looksmaxxing communities DHA self-tanner is discussed as a way to add colour without UV exposure, with threads on application mistakes, products and whether self-tanning is worthwhile compared to peptide tanning [4][5].
infobox: FDA-approved colour additive for topical use, not eyes, lips or mucous membranes [2]

paras: DHA is used to give a temporary tan on the face and body. Formulations include sprays, lotions, gels, mousses and cosmetic wipes, and salon applications include spray booths, airbrushing and hand-applied products. Lotions often last longer than sprays but may cause blotching and streaking, while mousses and gels tend to dry faster [1].

A review of vitiligo camouflage lists DHA among temporary concealment options [6]. Early research on DHA's skin colouring in the 1950s arose from observations in children given oral DHA for a glycogen storage disease [1]. A 1976 trial treated 30 photosensitive patients with a DHA and lawsone sunscreen [7], and a randomized study and registered trial have examined DHA for visible-light protection in erythropoietic protoporphyria [8][9].

Studies in humans have examined DHA's colouring and any photoprotective effect. A 2004 trial letter and a 2005 controlled study examined sunlight protection from DHA-induced Maillard-reaction pigments [10][11]. A 1976 clinical trial reported that a DHA-lawsone sunscreen protected 30 patients with various light sensitivities, with about 80 percent experiencing enough protection for a near-normal summer lifestyle [7]. A 2023 randomized trial examined protection against visible light by DHA in EPP [8], with a small registered follow-up [9].

Reviews state that sunless tanning products are regulated as cosmetics that cannot provide protection from UV, whereas earlier reviews describe DHA and melanins as providing some photoprotection [2][12]. There are no large randomized trials of DHA self-tanner as a cosmetic product comparing outcomes for appearance.

The FDA has approved DHA for topical use on the skin but not for the eyes, lips and mucous membranes; spray booths therefore raise concerns about exposure of these areas [1][2]. Reported effects of spray tans include rashes, cough, dizziness and fainting, and frequent exposure has been associated in the reference literature with possible respiratory disease risks [1]. Fragrances and preservatives in formulations may cause allergic reactions [1].
A systematic review of self-tanning agents notes concerns about DHA cytotoxicity, genotoxicity and systemic absorption. Reviews describe safety data on inhalation and long-term use as limited [2][3].

DHA condenses with amino-acid residues of keratin in the stratum corneum; the resulting melanoidins resemble melanin in colour and can be removed by abrasion. When injected, no pigmentation occurs, consistent with a role for oxygen in colour development [1]. It was initially thought not to penetrate past the stratum corneum, though the FDA later concluded this is not entirely true [1].

DHA is a hygroscopic white crystalline powder and the simplest ketose, with no chiral centre. It normally exists as a dimer that converts to the monomer in water, and solutions are stable at pH 4 to 6 but degrade to brown products in basic solution [1]. It is prepared by mild oxidation of glycerol or by fermentation, and can be derived from sugar beets and sugar cane [1][13]. Its phosphorylated form takes part in glycolysis [1].

German scientists recognised DHA as a skin-colouring agent in the 1920s after noticing browning when it was spilled during X-ray processing [1]. In the 1950s Eva Wittgenstein at the University of Cincinnati researched DHA, noting that children given large oral doses for glycogen storage disease developed brown skin where it was spilled, and then painted solutions on her own skin [1]. Coppertone introduced the first consumer sunless tanning lotion in the 1960s; many consumers disliked results such as orange palms and streaking, which shaped lingering associations with fake-looking tans [1]. The FDA added DHA to its list of approved cosmetic ingredients in the 1970s, and new formulations appeared in the 1980s [1].

On looksmax.org, threads include requests for help fixing streaky facial applications, product recommendations, questions about dose for self-tanning drops, and discussion of whether self-tanners suit people with many moles [4][14][15][5]. Some users recommend exfoliating with a scrub to remove uneven colour [4]. In one thread a poster asking about tanning with many moles was told to use melanotan 2, and another user replied that melanotan also raises melanocyte activity and may darken moles.

lore.intro: DHA is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a practical, low-commitment tanning option, often compared with sun exposure and melanotan [5].
